slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: An indirect proof (proof by contradiction) starts by assuming the opposite of what you want. If that leads to something impossible, the opposite is false, so the statement is true. Getting the opposite exactly right matters.

geo.title: The big idea

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• indirect proof A proof that assumes the opposite of what we want and shows that leads to something impossible.
  • contradiction Two statements that cannot both be true.
  • negation The 'not' version of a statement.
  • at least one One or more. Its opposite is 'none'.
  • none Not even one. Its opposite is 'at least one'.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Let n be an integer. Prove: if n² is odd, then n is odd.

Read the worked steps
StepReason

Since every integer is either even or odd, n = 2k for some integer k.Every integer is even or odd, and the definition of even.
Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²).Substitution and factoring.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Let n be an integer. Prove: if n² is odd, then n is odd.

steps.step: Let n be an integer and assume n² is odd. Suppose n is not odd.
steps.reason: Keep the given; assume the opposite of the conclusion.

steps.step: Since every integer is either even or odd, n = 2k for some integer k.
steps.reason: Every integer is even or odd, and the definition of even.

steps.step: Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²).
steps.reason: Substitution and factoring.

steps.step: Because k and 2 are integers, multiplication closure makes k² and 2k² integers.
steps.reason: Multiplication closure: an integer times an integer is an integer.

steps.step: Therefore n² is even.
steps.reason: Definition of even: 2 times an integer.

steps.step: But n² is odd. It can't be both even and odd.
steps.reason: This is the contradiction.

steps.step: So the assumption was false: n is odd.
steps.reason: Reject the opposite.

steps.step: Use it: if n² = 9, then n is 3 or -3. Both are odd, just as we proved. Testing n = 3 shows the idea; it does not replace the proof.
steps.reason: One example checks; the proof covers all cases.

steps.step: Second check: if n = 2k for an integer k, then n² = 2(2k²), and 2k² is an integer by multiplication closure, so n² is even. That is the contrapositive.
steps.reason: The same claim, seen from the other side.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Prove: no integer n solves 2n + 1 = 8.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Assume some integer n solves 2n + 1 = 8.Assume the opposite.
Then 2n = 7, so n = 7/2.Subtract 1, then divide by 2.
7/2 is not an integer, but we assumed n was.Contradiction.
So no integer solution exists.Reject the assumption.
Second check: for any integer n, 2n + 1 is odd, and 8 is even.Odd can never equal even.

steps.step: Assume some integer n solves 2n + 1 = 8.
steps.reason: Assume the opposite.

steps.step: Then 2n = 7, so n = 7/2.
steps.reason: Subtract 1, then divide by 2.

steps.step: 7/2 is not an integer, but we assumed n was.
steps.reason: Contradiction.

steps.step: So no integer solution exists.
steps.reason: Reject the assumption.

steps.step: Second check: for any integer n, 2n + 1 is odd, and 8 is even.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Leo thinks an indirect proof means 'proving the opposite is true.'

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

You assume the opposite only to show it breaks something. The proof ends by rejecting the opposite. Ask: what exactly does the contradiction clash with?

geo.title: Common mistake
geo.prompt: Leo thinks an indirect proof means 'proving the opposite is true.'
geo.correction: You assume the opposite only to show it breaks something. The proof ends by rejecting the opposite. Ask: what exactly does the contradiction clash with?

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Let n be an integer. Prove by contradiction: if n² is odd, then n is odd. Then use it when n² = 49, and test n = 7.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Let n be an integer and assume n² is odd. Suppose n is not odd. Since every integer is either even or odd, n = 2k for some integer k. Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²). Because k and 2 are integers, multiplication closure makes k² and 2k² integers. Therefore n² is even by the definition of even. This contradicts its being odd. Hence n is odd. If n² = 49, then n is 7 or -7, both odd. n = 7 is a check, not the proof.

Reveal second check

Contrapositive: if n = 2k for an integer k, then n² = 2(2k²), and 2k² is an integer by multiplication closure, so the square is even.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Ivy wants to prove 'some label is wrong.' She starts with 'Assume every label is wrong.' What should she assume instead?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Assume no label is wrong, which means every label is correct. 'Every label is wrong' is not the opposite of 'some label is wrong.'

Reveal second check

The opposite of 'there is at least one wrong label' is 'there are no wrong labels.'

geo.check: The opposite of 'there is at least one wrong label' is 'there are no wrong labels.'

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
In a made-up system, every object is red or blue, never both. Set L holds only red objects. Q is a blue object in set M. Prove by contradiction that L and M are different sets.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Assume L = M. Q is in M, so Q is in L, so Q is red. But Q is blue, and nothing is both. That is a contradiction, so L and M are different.

Reveal second check

A direct check: Q is in M but not in L. One member in one set and not the other shows the sets differ.
